slides.text: Veer Narayan Singh challenged the British policies even before the Revolt of 1857. The patriotic Zamindar of Sonakhan was martyred by the British Raj at the intersection of Raipur in the crime of sedition.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Jaistambh Chowk, Raipur, December 1857. Veer Narayan Singh standing before British cannons, head raised, unbroken. Crowds forced to watch. Dark colonial sky. Ink-wash illustration, ochre and charcoal palette. Tragedy and dignity.

slides.text: On May 10, 1857, a troop of soldiers filled with passion for independence revolted from Meerut and reached Delhi on May 11. Convincing Mirza Abu Zafar Siraj-ud-din Mohammad Bahadur Shah Zafar, they elected him their leader and crowned him again.
slides.visualDescription: The Red Fort, Delhi, May 1857. Rebel soldiers presenting themselves before the aged Bahadur Shah Zafar — 82 years old, confined to the Red Fort. His coronation. The slogans of Bahadur Shah Zafar Zindabad erupting across India. A spark becoming a fire.

slides.text: The news of Bahadur Shah Zafar being proclaimed emperor spread like a current across the country. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was a major but ultimately unsuccessful uprising against the rule of the British East India Company.
slides.visualDescription: The news spreading across India — from Delhi to Lucknow to Kanpur to Chhattisgarh. A current of electric energy moving across the map. Each city lighting up as the rebellion reaches it. The geography of 1857 made visual. Fire spreading.

slides.text: Sonakhan village, Chhattisgarh. 1856. A severe famine grips the land. Veer Narayan Singh — Zamindar of Sonakhan — goes to the moneylender asking for grain for his starving people. The moneylender refuses.
slides.visualDescription: Sonakhan village in famine — cracked earth, thin cattle, hollow-eyed villagers. Veer Narayan Singh — a man of bearing and conscience — standing before a fat moneylender surrounded by full grain sacks. The refusal. Moral clarity facing greed.

slides.text: When the moneylender refused to give food grains, Veer Narayan Singh broke open the godown and distributed the grains to the public. The incident was reported to Deputy Commissioner Elliot. Narayan Singh was arrested on false charges of traitor and robber.
slides.visualDescription: Veer Narayan Singh breaking the lock of the moneylender's godown. Grain pouring out. Starving villagers' hands reaching forward to receive it. A revolutionary act of conscience. Then: British officers arriving to arrest him. Right made crime.

slides.text: In 1857, as the news of Bahadur Shah Zafar's overthrow spread, the independence of the rebellion intensified. The people of Chhattisgarh accepted the jailed Veer Narayan Singh as their leader and joined in the rebellion.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur jail — news of 1857 reaching through its walls. Veer Narayan Singh inside, the people outside rallying around his name. His imprisonment becoming his election as leader. The jail as a pedestal rather than a cage. The people choosing.

slides.text: With the help of soldiers of the British Army at Raipur, Veer Narayan Singh escaped from prison. He reached Sonakhan and formed an army of 500 men. He was determined to revolt against the growing atrocities of the British.
slides.visualDescription: The dramatic prison escape — Veer Narayan Singh slipping out of Raipur jail with help from sympathetic soldiers. Running through the night toward Sonakhan. Then: 500 men assembled on the banks of the river, weapons raised, a leader before his army.

slides.text: A powerful British army was dispatched to crush the Sonakhan army. Under the leadership of Smith, it crushed the Sonakhan revolt and apprehended Narayan Singh again. He was prosecuted for rebelling against the British Raj.
slides.visualDescription: The British army advancing on Sonakhan — modern weapons, organised formations against Veer Narayan Singh's 500 men with traditional weapons. The battle. The capture. Smith's forces surrounding Sonakhan. The second arrest. Inevitable but undefeated.

slides.text: Veer Narayan Singh was blown up in the middle of Raipur City on the charge of rebelling against the British Raj. The place where Veer Narayan was martyred is currently known as Jaistambh Chowk in Raipur near the Kaiser-e-Hind Darwaza.
slides.visualDescription: Jaistambh Chowk, December 10, 1857. The intersection of Raipur. British cannon. Veer Narayan Singh brought forward. The execution — designed as a spectacle of terror. Instead: an act of consecration. The chowk becoming holy ground.

slides.text: All the soldiers of Raipur were ordered to be present to see this. This was done so that the people became terrorized and did not dare to raise their heads against the British. The strategy backfired — it lit a fuse instead.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur soldiers standing in formation, forced to witness the execution. Their faces — fear, grief, barely suppressed rage. The British officers watching with satisfaction. The satisfaction misplaced. Among those watching soldiers: Hanuman Singh.

slides.text: Thirty-nine days later, on January 18, 1858, a group of soldiers revolted against the British. At that time there was a military cantonment in Raipur — the Third Regular Regiment. Some Faizis planned an armed attack on the night of January 18, at 7:30 p.m.
slides.visualDescription: Night of January 18, 1858. The Raipur military cantonment. Darkness and torchlight. Soldier Hanuman Singh moving toward the chamber of Sergeant Major Sidbell. 7:30 pm. The clock on the cantonment wall. The moment of no return approaching.

slides.text: Soldier Hanuman Singh inflicted several fatal blows on Sergeant Major Sidbell of the Third Regiment of the Native Infantry, who was at that time resting alone in his chamber, killing him in a short time.
slides.visualDescription: The chamber of Sergeant Major Sidbell — Hanuman Singh entering, the confrontation. Dramatic, tense, dark interior. The act of rebellion in its most personal form. A soldier choosing country over orders. The cost of that choice already written in his fate.

slides.text: This 18-man contingent reached the camp after the killing and invited other soldiers to join the rebellion. The other soldiers did not agree. By the time the news of the killing had spread, the British officers were alert, surrounding all 18 soldiers from all sides.
slides.visualDescription: The 18 rebel soldiers in the cantonment, trying to convince others to join. Fellow soldiers stepping back, afraid. British officers rallying, surrounding them. The isolation of the rebels — 18 against an empire. Surrounded but not surrendered.

slides.text: After firing that lasted for about 6–7 hours, the rebel soldiers ran out of cartridges. Meanwhile, Hanuman Singh, the main accused, escaped. But all the other 17 accomplices were arrested by the British.
slides.visualDescription: Six hours of gunfire in the dark Raipur cantonment. Cartridges running out. 17 soldiers captured. Hanuman Singh slipping away into the darkness of Chhattisgarh's night. The last cartridge spent. Silence falling. Capture. Escape.

slides.text: Those who were tried were all sentenced to death for the crime of rebellion. They were hanged on 22 February 1858 in the presence of all the soldiers of the army.
slides.visualDescription: February 22, 1858. The 17 soldiers standing before the gallows in the Raipur cantonment. All of the army's soldiers forced to watch again. The British repeating their tactic of making martyrdom a spectacle — again it will fail. Somber, powerful.

slides.text: The seventeen martyrs: Ghazi Khan, Havaldar Badlu, Hayat Golanadaj, Munim, Shivnarayan, Pannalal, Maatadin, Bukaram, Bilhu, Akbar Hussain, Lalsingh, Bablu, Paranand, Shobharam, Durgaprasad, Nazar Muhammad, Shiva, Devidin Golanadaj.
slides.visualDescription: The names of the 17 martyrs appearing one by one — Hindu, Muslim, people of all faiths and communities. Each name lit like a star. The diversity of the sacrifice: Ghazi Khan and Shivnarayan, Akbar Hussain and Pannalal — dying together for one country.

slides.text: People of all castes and religions were among the seventeen martyrs of the rebellion — which is a symbol of the great sense of national interest instilled in the people of this region. One nation in one sacrifice.
slides.visualDescription: The 17 names arranged in a circle — Hindu and Muslim names alternating, a visual statement of unity in sacrifice. Different communities, one purpose. The most powerful rebuke to those who would divide India by faith: these men died as one.

slides.text: Hanuman Singh had also tried to attack the bungalow of the Deputy Commissioner of Chhattisgarh on the night of January 20, 1858, two days after the rebellion. The British government announced a cash reward of Rs 500 for his arrest.
slides.visualDescription: Wanted posters for Hanuman Singh posted across Raipur — Rs 500 reward. British patrols searching. The Deputy Commissioner's bungalow with extra guards. Hanuman Singh nowhere to be found. A man who became a ghost. The empire unable to cage him.

slides.text: Despite the lure of such a huge amount, he could not be arrested. After this incident of the escape of Hanuman Singh, no details of him were received. He never came back. Like Gundadhur, he walked into history and did not return.
slides.visualDescription: Hanuman Singh's footprints in the dust of Raipur — leading away from the city, into the countryside, growing fainter. Then nothing. The trail ending. The man becoming legend. Another hero absorbed by the land that made him.

slides.text: Surendra Sai, freedom fighter of 1857, was the rightful heir of the princely state of Sambalpur. His activity spread from Sambalpur to Bilaspur and Kalahandi. He troubled the British greatly in the revolt of 1857.
slides.visualDescription: Surendra Sai leading his rebellion across a vast territory — from Sambalpur through Bilaspur to Kalahandi. The map showing the breadth of his resistance. A regional uprising of scale. A man whose territory of defiance was larger than many kingdoms.

slides.text: Surendra Sai was arrested from his house on 13 January 1862. Sent from Raipur Jail to Nagpur Jail and then to Asirgarh Fort. He died a natural death on 23 May 1884 in Asirgarh. At last, he went blind.
slides.visualDescription: The long arc of Surendra Sai's imprisonment — Raipur jail, then Nagpur jail, then Asirgarh Fort. Each transfer moving him further from home. An old man going blind in a fortress. Twenty-two years of imprisonment. Dignity outlasting the body.

slides.text: Although Veer Surendra Sai died a natural death, in honor of his valor, people call him The Last Martyr of the Revolt of 1857. His name links the 1857 uprising to everything that came after in Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Surendra Sai's portrait — blind, aged, yet dignified. The title: The Last Martyr of 1857. A bridge between two eras of resistance. His blindness a metaphor for all that history refused to see. Honor in death that was denied in life.

slides.text: In the revolution of 1857, the king of Sarangarh supported the British government. The revolutionary Kamal Singh was tricked and handed over to the British. In 1867, Kamal Singh was hanged — betrayed by those who should have been his allies.
slides.visualDescription: The betrayal at Sarangarh — Kamal Singh being handed over to British officers by the king who chose colonial comfort. The revolutionary's face as he realises what has happened. Then: 1867, the gallows at Sarangarh. Betrayal as a form of violence.

slides.text: The fire of freedom never extinguished in this region. As a spark within the pile of ashes, it kept smoldering, erupting sometimes in Rajnandgaon under Sevata Thakur, sometimes in Sarguja under the Bagud Baniya.
slides.visualDescription: Chhattisgarh's map at night — multiple embers glowing at different points. Rajnandgaon, Sarguja, Kawardha, Bastar. The geography of persistent resistance. Each ember a name, a story, a refusal to surrender. The land as a living archive.

slides.text: In Chhattisgarh, the national level movements were in effect and were led by freedom fighters of the state — starting with the revolution of 1857 which continued till the attainment of independence of India in 1947.
slides.visualDescription: A timeline from 1857 to 1947 — ninety years of continuous resistance in Chhattisgarh. Each decade marked with a name, an event, a sacrifice. The longest fight. The most patient people. The freedom of 1947 as the inheritance of 1857.

slides.text: Jaistambh Chowk in Raipur — the place where Veer Narayan Singh was martyred — stands today as a living reminder. Near the Kaiser-e-Hind Darwaza, on the ground where blood was shed, a city continues its daily life over a sacred wound.
slides.visualDescription: Present-day Jaistambh Chowk, Raipur — traffic, people, modern buildings. But the chowk itself unchanged in spirit. A ghost of 1857 visible in the architecture. The present moving over the past. History underfoot. Sacred ground unmarked but remembered.

slides.text: Veer Narayan Singh — the Zamindar who broke a godown to feed the starving, who escaped prison to lead an army, who was executed publicly to terrorize others. He achieved the opposite of what his executioners intended.
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of Veer Narayan Singh — strong, righteous, looking ahead. The grain he distributed still metaphorically feeding the movement. The jail he escaped still standing while his name is free. The cannon that killed him now a symbol of the empire's failure.

slides.text: The 17 soldiers who were hanged. Hanuman Singh who vanished. Surendra Sai who went blind in a fortress. Kamal Singh who was betrayed. Each one a different shape of the same sacrifice — the refusal to accept that another man's flag should fly over your land.
slides.visualDescription: Four images in a grid: the 17 soldiers at the gallows, Hanuman Singh's disappearing footprints, Surendra Sai blind in Asirgarh, Kamal Singh betrayed. Four shapes of sacrifice. Four ways to die for one idea. The idea: that this is our land.

slides.text: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was ultimately unsuccessful as a military campaign. But as a declaration of intent — as proof that the people of this land would not stop — it was the most successful statement in Indian history.
slides.visualDescription: The British flag still flying over Chhattisgarh after 1857 — the rebellion suppressed. But below it, in the streets and villages, something has changed. Eyes that no longer look down. A people who now know they can fight. The victory beneath the defeat.

slides.text: The third era of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement begins now. No longer armed revolt alone — but organised political consciousness. Leaders emerge who fight with words, with newspapers, with Congress sessions, with Satyagraha.
slides.visualDescription: The transition: swords and spears being set aside, pens and newspapers taking their place. A printing press beginning to run. Newspapers with anti-British headlines. A Congress session being organised. The new weapons of the new era taking shape.

slides.text: From the soil watered by the blood of Veer Narayan Singh, Gaind Singh, Gundadhur, and the 17 soldiers — from this red soil — new leaders will grow. They will not carry bows and arrows. They will carry something more dangerous: organised truth.
slides.visualDescription: Red Chhattisgarh soil — the same soil where the martyrs fell. From it, green shoots growing upward. Each shoot becoming a leader of the next era — Pt. Sundarlal Sharma, Ravi Shankar Shukla, Chhotelal Srivastava. Blood becomes roots becomes growth.

slides.text: Madhavrao Sapre will start a newspaper. Sundarlal Sharma will fight untouchability. Ravi Shankar Shukla will organise a Congress committee. The revolution will not always be visible — but it will never stop.
slides.visualDescription: Three panels: Sapre at a printing press, Sharma at a temple entrance with Harijans, Shukla at a Congress table. Three forms of the same resistance. Ink-wash illustration, 1900s aesthetic, the new generation of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement.

slides.text: The cannon at Jaistambh was meant to end resistance. Instead it announced it. Every cannon shot that kills a man of conscience adds ten more to his cause. The British were learning this lesson slowly, at great cost to Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: The cannon at Jaistambh Chowk — smoke clearing after the shot. In the smoke, ten new faces of resistance appearing. The mathematics of martyrdom: one taken, many rising. The British miscalculation made visible as a visual equation.

slides.text: The freedom struggle of 1857 was crushed. But the fire of freedom never extinguished in this region. As a spark within the pile of ashes, it kept smoldering, erupting at different times and different places.
slides.visualDescription: Ashes of the 1857 rebellion — cooling, grey, apparently dead. Then: the ember deep within, pulsing. The Gazetteer's words on screen: the freedom struggle was crushed. But underneath those official words, the truth: it was not. The spark lives.

slides.text: They all became revolutionary martyrs. Their names fill this ground. Their sacrifice fills this soil. And in 1900, a man named Madhavrao Sapre begins publishing a newspaper called Chhattisgarh Mitra — and the awakening takes a new form.
slides.visualDescription: The first issue of Chhattisgarh Mitra, 1900 — fresh ink on paper. Madhavrao Sapre holding it up in lamplight. The names of the 1857 martyrs fading into the background as the newspaper comes forward. Words replacing weapons. The awakening continues.

slides.text: From the first martyr Gaind Singh in 1825 to Veer Narayan Singh in 1857 to the 17 soldiers in 1858 to Surendra Sai in 1884 — each generation of Chhattisgarh paid its price. Now a new generation inherits the debt and the determination.
slides.visualDescription: A genealogy of sacrifice — portraits from each era arranged in sequence: 1825, 1857, 1858, 1884, 1910. Each face passing a torch to the next. The torch now arriving in the hands of a new generation — the Gandhian era leaders waiting.

slides.text: The fire of armed revolt dims. A new kind of warrior emerges — one who fights with truth, with discipline, with sacrifice without violence. Their leader is coming. Next: Episode 5 — Awakening.
slides.visualDescription: Dawn over Chhattisgarh — the first light of the 20th century touching the Sal forests and the forts. A new day. A new method. The charkha beginning to turn in a dark room, its thread catching the morning light. Title: Episode 5 — Awakening.
